newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Kabila's Congo targets self-reliance, farm growth.
newsitem.headline: Kabila's Congo targets self-reliance, farm growth.

text.p: Laurent Kabila's Congo, preaching self-reliance within a social market economy, plans to promote agriculture, fishing and cattle-breeding as the main motor of growth.

National Reconstruction Minister Etienne Mbaya, outlining government plans at the end of a two-week reconstruction and development conference in the capital Kinshasa, said they would resort to technology tailored to the nation's specific needs.
"We will make agriculture, cattle breeding and fishing the main source of the country's economy growth," he told 1,200 Congolese delegates on Saturday at the closing ceremony.

The Democratic Republic of the Congo, the former Zaire, is Africa's third largest country and potentially one of its richest, with a wealth of minerals, rich farmland and the hydroelectric potential to light up much of the continent.
Over three decades of corruption and mismanagement under ousted dictator Mobutu Sese Seko left its more than 40 million people among Africa's poorest.
With official statistics lacking, many economist say unemployment hovers at about 70 percent of the workforce.
Many people scratch a living in the informal sector, trading anything from home-grown vegetables to currency and cigarettes.

Kabila, who proclaimed himself president in May after his Rwandan-backed forces toppled Kabila in a lightning seven-month campaign, inherited a foreign debt of around $14 billion and a crumbling and, in some places, non-existent infrastructure.
He pledged in his inauguration speech that the government would rehabilitate the nation's social and economic fabric.

"The challenge of the reconstruction of transport and communications infrastructures... can be met if only we rely on ourselves but not on foreign aid," Mbaya said. "We will chiefly count on our own resources and on technology adapted to our social, cultural and economic context."
Mining -- copper, cobalt, diamonds, gold and other minerals -- was at the heart of Zaire's economy, although much of the wealth it generated was siphoned off by Mobutu and his cronies.
State mining giant Gecamines, its main foreign currency earner, has seen annual production slump from 500,000 tonnes of copper in the mid-1980s to about 30,000 tonnes in 1996.
Kabila has been in touch with investors interested in the potentially lucrative mining sector. Some deals have been signed but caution seems to be the watch-word on both sides.
"The terms of trade of raw materials with Western countries are unfair," Mbaya said.
One idea floated by ministers has been to tie potentially lucrative mining contracts into infrastructure projects such as road building -- a government target in each region.
Major Western donors had foresaken Zaire for human rights violations and lack of democracy under Mobutu. They say aid can resume if Kabila improves the nation's human rights record.
The World Bank plans to convene a meeting of donors in September. The government has said that in the meantime no foreign debt will be paid back.
The government is also keen to bring home what remains of the billions of dollars reputedly stashed away by Mobutu and his cronies and use the money to revive the economy.
In the meantime, it says it wants to get the nation back to work. "What counts is to resume production," Mbaya said.
A repeat conference is planned before the end of the year.
